data.name: Grilled Salmon Ochazuke With Sencha
data.description: Tender flakes of grilled salmon crown warm Japanese rice with crisp nori and toasted sesame. Hot sencha brings a grassy aroma and gentle astringency to this light, savory bowl.

refrigerator.notes: Store rice and salmon separately from tea and dry toppings. Cool promptly in shallow containers and refrigerate within 1 hour at 4°C (40°F) or below. Eat within 24 hours. Assembled bowls soften quickly and are best eaten immediately.

freezer.notes: Freezing the assembled dish is not recommended because the rice becomes waterlogged and the nori loses its texture.

storage.reheating: Reheat stored rice and salmon separately until each reaches 74°C (165°F) throughout. Add freshly heated green tea and dry toppings immediately before serving. Hot tea alone is not a reliable way to reheat refrigerated leftovers.

items.name: salmon
items.notes: Edible flesh weight; use two 120 g portions approximately 2 cm thick.

items.name: canola oil
items.notes: For lightly coating the salmon before grilling.

items.name: salt
items.notes: Use unsalted salmon so this seasoning amount remains appropriate.

items.name: cooked short-grain white rice
items.notes: Prepared weight. Use freshly cooked warm rice or promptly refrigerated rice no more than 24 hours old. The total recipe time assumes the rice is already cooked.

items.name: brewed green tea
items.notes: Prepared beverage weight after removing the leaves. Use regular caffeinated sencha; the served infusion contains caffeine. The total recipe time assumes the tea is already brewed.

items.name: nori
items.preparation: plain toasted, torn into small pieces

instructions.text: Preheat the grill pan over medium heat for about 4 minutes.
Coat the salmon evenly with the oil and salt on the plate for raw salmon. Wash your hands after handling the fish, and keep the raw-fish plate away from the rice, toppings and cooked salmon.

Grill the salmon for approximately 4–5 minutes per side, turning with the fish spatula, until the thickest part reaches 63°C (145°F). Wash the spatula after its last contact with undercooked fish before using it to remove the cooked salmon.

doneness_cues.visual: The flesh is opaque and separates into moist flakes; the surface has light grill marks.

tips: Check the temperature through the side of each portion so the thermometer tip reaches its center.

instructions.text: If using refrigerated rice, reheat it in the microwave-safe bowl under its vented lid, using short intervals and stirring between them, until it reaches 74°C (165°F) throughout, approximately 3–4 minutes. Freshly cooked rice can be used while still hot.

doneness_cues.visual: Steam rises throughout the rice with no cool clumps.

tips: Do this while the salmon grills.

instructions.text: Warm the brewed sencha in the small saucepan to approximately 80°C (176°F), without boiling.
tips: Warm the tea while the salmon finishes cooking.

instructions.text: Flake the cooked salmon into bite-size pieces with the fork on the clean plate, checking for and removing any remaining pin bones.
Divide the hot rice between the serving bowls and arrange equal portions of salmon, nori and sesame seeds over each.
Pour half the hot green tea around the rice in each bowl and serve immediately.

troubleshooting.symptom: The tea tastes bitter and overwhelms the salmon.
troubleshooting.likely_cause: The sencha was brewed too strongly or left in contact with the leaves too long.
troubleshooting.prevention: Use a light, freshly strained sencha infusion and warm it gently without boiling.
troubleshooting.fix: Before assembling the bowls, replace the bitter tea with the same weight of more gently brewed sencha.

troubleshooting.likely_cause: The portions were thin or cooked well beyond their safe temperature.
troubleshooting.prevention: Use evenly thick portions and check the center temperature near the end of grilling.
troubleshooting.fix: Flake the salmon into smaller pieces and moisten it with the hot tea when serving; lost moisture cannot be fully restored.

chef_notes: Keep the salmon flakes fairly large so their moist centers contrast with the individual rice grains.
Add the nori immediately before pouring the tea; its toasted aroma fades as it sits in liquid.

Regular brewed sencha contains caffeine even after its leaves are removed. Caffeine content varies with the tea and brewing method. See the [IFIC caffeine reference](https://ific.org/resources/caffeine-calculator/).

Cook fresh salmon to 63°C (145°F), and reheat leftover salmon and rice to 74°C (165°F), following [FoodSafety.gov temperature guidance](https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/safe-minimum-internal-temperatures).
data.cultural_context: Ochazuke is a Japanese rice dish served with hot tea or dashi and savory toppings, often enjoyed as a simple meal or a meal's closing course. Salmon, nori and sesame are familiar toppings, as described in [Just One Cookbook's ochazuke guide](https://www.justonecookbook.com/ochazuke/).
